title: Tracing Table
body:
Executing the code by hand, one row per step, one column per variable. **You are the computer**,
and the table is what you write down because you cannot hold five variables in your head at once.

```python
total = 0
i = 1
while i <= 4:
    total = total + i
    i = i + 1
```

| Step | `i` | `total` | `i <= 4` |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| initial | 1 | 0 | |
| test | 1 | 0 | True |
| body | 2 | 1 | |
| test | 2 | 1 | True |
| body | 3 | 3 | |
| test | 3 | 3 | True |
| body | 4 | 6 | |
| test | 4 | 6 | True |
| body | 5 | 10 | |
| test | 5 | 10 | **False**, exit |

The condition gets its own column deliberately. Loop bugs are almost always about **when the test
is evaluated relative to the update**, and putting both in the table is what makes an off-by-one
visible rather than arguable. See [[Control variable]] and [[Loop design]].

**This is the technique for [[Logic Errors]]**, the class of bug where the program runs happily
and produces the wrong answer, so nothing tells you anything. A tracing table finds them by
comparing what the code does against what you meant at every step, which is the only method that
works when there is no error message to read. [[debugging]] covers the tool-assisted version;
this is the pen-and-paper one, and it is faster on short code than setting up a debugger.

Trace an [[Infinite loop]] and the table shows you the reason directly: some column stops
changing, or the condition column never reaches False.
